title: The article and the prefixed particles

objectives.can: Separate a prefixed article, preposition or conjunction from its word and name it.

explanation.summary: Hebrew has a definite article, written on the front of the noun, but no word for 'a'. It also writes 'and', 'in', 'to', 'like' and 'from' as single letters fastened to the next word. Almost every line of the Bible has some of these, so reading begins with peeling them off.

sections.heading: One article, and only a definite one
body: The article is הַ, fastened to the front of a noun or adjective. It does not change for gender or number: the same article stands before a masculine, a feminine, a singular or a plural word. Compare אֶרֶץ, 'earth, land', with הָאָרֶץ, 'the earth'.
There is no indefinite article. A noun with no article may be translated 'a …' or just 'land', 'light', 'darkness', as the sense asks. The absence of the article never means 'a' by itself.
The article is not a separate word. In the word-by-word display it appears as a feature of the whole word, Definite.

sections.heading: How the article looks
body: After the ה the first letter of the noun is usually doubled, and a dagesh (a dot inside the letter) shows it: הַשָּׁמַיִם, 'the heavens'. The letters א and ר, and often ע, cannot be doubled in this way, so the vowel before them is lengthened instead: הָאָרֶץ, הָרָקִיעַ, הָעִיר. Before ח the article is usually הַ and nothing is doubled: הַחֹשֶׁךְ, 'the darkness'. Before a few words with an unstressed first syllable beginning ע or ה the article is הֶ: הֶעָרִים, הֶהָרִים.
Do not try to memorise all this at once. What matters is that every one of these spellings is the article, and that the vowel under ה is a, ā or e depending on the letter that follows.

sections.heading: The prefixed particles
body: Five very common little words are not written apart from their noun. They are single letters with a short vowel, usually a shewa, joined to the front: וְ 'and', בְּ 'in, at, with', לְ 'to, for', כְּ 'like, as', and מִ 'from, out of' (the beginning of the separate word מִן). They can stand before any noun, adjective, pronoun or verb. In the word display they appear as the feature Prefix.

When one of these meets a word that has the article, ב, ל and כ take over the article's place and its vowel, and the ה disappears. So בְּ + הָאָרֶץ is written בָּאָרֶץ, 'in the land', and לְ + הָאוֹר is written לָאוֹר, 'to the light'. The article is still there, but you can see it only in the vowel; the corpus records it as Definite. The particles וְ and מִ never hide the article: with the article they are וְהָאָרֶץ and מֵהָעוֹף.
Particles can pile up: ו may stand in front of another particle. וּבַבְּהֵמָה means 'and in the animal', and has three parts: ו, then ב, then the article.

sections.heading: The forms of 'and' and of 'from'
body: The conjunction is וְ before most words. Before the letters ב, מ, פ and before a word that begins with a shewa it is וּ, pronounced like 'oo': וּבֵין, וּשְׁנֵי. These are still the same 'and'.

The preposition 'from' is the word מִן on its own, but as a prefix it is usually מִ with the next letter doubled, or מֵ before letters that cannot be doubled (א, ע, ר and often ה, ח): מִבֵּית, 'from the house of', and מֵאֶרֶץ, 'from the land of'.

sections.heading: Working backwards
body: To read a long word, strip it from the front. First look for ו. Then look for ב, ל, כ or מ. Then ask whether what remains is a noun with the article. The word you reach is the noun.

Letters that look like prefixes may belong to the noun. The ב of בֵּן 'son', the ל of לֵב 'heart' and the מ of מַיִם 'water' are part of those words. The word display, and a dictionary, tell you which is which.

misunderstandings: The vowel of לָאוֹר is not a sign that a ה is missing by accident. It is the article, absorbed into the ל; the word means 'to the light', not 'to light'.
A noun without the article is not automatically 'a …'. Names, materials and things spoken of in general often have no article in Hebrew, and English adds one or leaves it out.
וְ, בְּ, לְ, כְּ and מִ are not nouns or separate words, even though English translates each with a word. Their meaning is real, but they cannot be written alone.
The article does not agree with the noun in gender or number. It is the same הַ everywhere; only its vowel changes, and only because of the letter that follows.

deeper.heading: Why the ה falls out
body: Grammarians describe it this way: when ב, ל or כ is put before the article, the ה drops out and the particle takes the article's vowel. That is why בָּאָרֶץ has the same vowels as הָאָרֶץ. After וְ and מִ the ה stays. This is a description of the written forms, and it is enough for reading.

examples.analysis: לָאוֹר is ל + the article + אוֹר: 'to the light'. You can see that the article is there only because of the vowel under the ל and the lengthened vowel after it. וְלַחֹשֶׁךְ is two prefixes and the article: 'and to the darkness'.
